# Basic Statistics {.unnumbered}

_Written for this book by Giorgio Arcara, with an AI assistant (Claude). This part is not in Irizarry's *Introduction to Data Science*._

This part of the book is a short refresher of the basic statistics you have probably met in earlier courses: how to summarize the centre and the spread of a list of numbers, how to describe the association between two variables with a correlation, how to compare two groups with the t-test and the Wilcoxon test, how to compare more than two groups with an ANOVA, how to deal with multiple comparisons, how to test the association between two categorical variables with the chi-square test, and, for all these tests, how to measure the size of an effect and how to plan the sample size of a study with a power analysis. It is meant to be read rather than studied as a separate topic: the course refers to these chapters whenever a concept such as the standard deviation or the correlation coefficient is used, so that you can check its definition quickly. The chapters use the same `behdslabs` datasets as the rest of the book. The ideas behind statistical inference, such as standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values, are explained in the earlier parts of this book, on probability and inference, and these chapters link back to them. If you want a fuller treatment, several excellent books are freely available online: Danielle Navarro's [*Learning Statistics with R*](https://learningstatisticswithr.com/), written for psychology students; Russell Poldrack's [*Statistical Thinking for the 21st Century*](https://statsthinking21.github.io/statsthinking21-core-site/); and Daniël Lakens' [*Improving Your Statistical Inferences*](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/), which focuses on p-values, effect sizes and confidence intervals. Each chapter ends with pointers to the relevant sections.
